prompt.context: Two of your business school classmates, despite trends indicating otherwise, decided to open a video rental store near the HBS campus. Their first two and a half years met unprecedented success — they bought matching Porsches and a townhouse in Beacon Hill. However, about 12 months ago, profits dramatically fell despite earlier strong revenue and profit growth. They have called you for help, saying they don't know what happened and that their mortgage and car payments are getting harder to meet.
prompt.question: What do you think the problem is?

clarifying_info.a: No, costs have not significantly increased.

clarifying_info.q: Have new video stores opened in the area?
clarifying_info.a: No, no new video stores have opened.

clarifying_info.q: Are fewer customers coming to the store?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — traffic data shows that fewer customers are coming into the store.

clarifying_info.q: Are customers renting fewer videos per visit (share of wallet)?
clarifying_info.a: Traffic has fallen, not spend per customer. It is a traffic problem, not a share-of-wallet problem.

clarifying_info.q: Have new movie theatres opened in the area?
clarifying_info.a: No, no new movie theatres have opened.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been economic changes in the area?
clarifying_info.a: Video rentals are generally not highly sensitive to economic factors; this is unlikely to be the primary driver.

framework: Diagnose whether the profit decline is driven by revenue decline or cost increase
Decompose revenue into price x volume (customers x videos per customer)
Determine whether the traffic/volume issue is internal (execution) or external (competitive/market)
Define the competitive set broadly: the client is in home movie entertainment, not just video store rental
Identify macro or competitive shifts in the home entertainment market that could be drawing customers away

questions.prompt: If profits have declined, what are the two possible drivers?
questions.guidance: Either revenues have declined or costs have increased. In a high-fixed-cost business like video rental (rent, inventory, labor are largely fixed relative to rental revenue), profits are highly sensitive to revenue changes. Cost is less likely to be the culprit here. Confirm that revenues have in fact fallen.

questions.prompt: Revenues have decreased. How would you decompose the revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Revenue = number of videos rented x price per rental. Since prices have not changed, the decline must come from fewer videos being rented. This can be further split into (a) fewer customers visiting the store (traffic problem) or (b) each customer renting fewer videos per visit (share-of-wallet problem).

questions.prompt: How would you determine whether it is a traffic problem or a share-of-wallet problem?
questions.guidance: The security system likely has a door counter that tracks store traffic. Register receipts can show the number of videos rented per transaction per day. Comparing this year versus last year isolates whether the issue is traffic (external/market) or share-of-wallet (internal/execution). The data shows traffic has fallen — it is a traffic problem.

questions.prompt: Traffic has fallen. What hypotheses would you form about the cause?
questions.guidance: Traffic decline is typically external: macro factors or competitive dynamics. Video rentals are relatively insensitive to economic cycles, so competitive factors are more likely. Initial hypotheses: new video store opened nearby, new movie theatre opened. Both are ruled out. The student should broaden the competitive set definition.

questions.prompt: How would you define the client's business and competitive set?
questions.guidance: The client is not simply in the 'video store' business — they are in the home movie entertainment business. The competitive set therefore includes anyone who provides movies at home: cable TV, pay-per-view (PPV), video-on-demand (VOD), DVD delivery services, and emerging movie-on-demand / streaming technology. A shift to any of these would reduce foot traffic without a new physical store opening nearby.

brainstorming.prompt: What potential competitive or market forces could be reducing customer traffic to a video rental store?

categories.name: Broadcast and cable expansion
ideas: New premium cable channels offering more movie content
Free broadcast TV movie blocks growing

categories.name: Consumer behavior shifts
ideas: Preference for convenience of at-home ordering over driving to a store
Shift to ownership (DVD purchasing) rather than rental
Binge-watching habits emerging with broader content availability

categories.name: Technology adoption
ideas: Faster internet enabling reliable video downloads
Smart TVs and set-top boxes making on-demand easy
Gaming consoles providing video rental/streaming capabilities

recommendation: The most likely cause of the traffic decline is the growth of in-home movie delivery and on-demand technology (cable VOD, PPV, delivery services, or early streaming), which has reduced the addressable market for physical video rental stores near HBS
The business model is structurally threatened by disruptive substitutes, not by a single competitor opening nearby
risks: The trend toward digital/on-demand delivery is secular and likely to accelerate, not reverse
High fixed-cost structure means even a moderate traffic decline has an outsized impact on profitability
Location near a university campus may mean the customer base is early adopters of new technology, accelerating the shift
next_steps: Quantify the traffic decline year-over-year to size the revenue gap
Survey or interview lapsed customers to confirm which substitutes they have switched to
Evaluate whether the business can pivot (e.g., add gaming rentals, become a pick-up point for a delivery service, or expand into niche/specialty content not available on digital platforms)
Model the economics under continued traffic decline to determine if the store remains viable
